items.gist: The passage opens the topic of diverse śaktipāta and states that an opponent's view will first be shown and then refuted.
It presents the view that the variegated world of pleasure, pain, and delusion arises from inert matter agitated by the Lord.
Objections are raised about karma-saṃskāras, the destruction of karma by knowledge, and the Lord's relation to karma.
Ajñāna is treated as cooperating with karma to produce fruits such as heaven, while knowledge destroys it.
The debate examines whether ajñāna is prior non-existence or destruction, with difficulties for both positions.
An alternative false-knowledge view is considered, along with problems concerning karma, dissolution, and rebirth.
The discussion turns to dissolution, the nature of atoms, and the Sāṃkhya pradhāna.
Buddhi, experience, and the relation between the person and enjoyment are analyzed.
The limits of bhoga and viveka are discussed, concluding that the Sāṃkhya account of ajñāna is untenable.
Ajñāna is described as a covering of the conscious atoms, identified with māyā.
Māyā is argued to be one eternal, inert impurity bound to all selves and the seed of saṃsāra.
When Śiva's power removes the obstruction, the atom is touched and śaktipāta occurs.
The mala theory is refuted through problems of its destruction, causation, and the unacceptable consequence that liberated beings would not be free.
